clarity.justification: The experiments closely match the proposed dissociation: Experiment 3 tests whether harm is shared, Experiment 4 compares whether “harm-patch flips <=15% while the language/threshold-signal patch flips >=50%,” and Experiment 5 tests whether a recovered direction “closes >=50% of the refusal gap.” The many directional, numeric criteria make all three central hypotheses decisively falsifiable, including “coverage not stronger, or gap <0.05 = refuted” and “If harm-patching flips more, H2 is refuted.” The remaining gap is that the relationship among the “per-language crossover severity,” the activation projection called a threshold, and the proposed “late-layer language-identity/threshold signal” is not fully specified, so successful patching or steering would not by itself uniquely identify a single scalar gate rather than a broader language-conditioned refusal mechanism.

feasibility.justification: The hardest step is to “patch A's late-layer language-identity/threshold signal into B,” because the plan does not specify exactly how that signal is isolated from other language-dependent activation differences; this requires custom identification logic rather than being a fully specified standard patching operation. The named artifacts—“Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B-Instruct,” AdvBench, HarmBench, XSTest, lang2vec, linear probes, activation patching, and refusal-direction extraction—exist and are supported by standard interpretability and statistical tooling, although the “validated multilingual refusal classifier” is not identified concretely. Resources and scale are unusually well quantified (“150 base harmful intents,” “600 graded items,” “250 matched clearly-benign controls,” “15 languages,” “3 paraphrase seeds,” and “human spot-checks on 5%”), while random-direction, benign, translation, paraphrase, logit-editing, and matched-item controls make negative outcomes runnable.
